text: Chapter 3 covered KPIs and dashboards — the ongoing "is governance healthy this month" view. A maturity assessment asks a slower-moving question instead: how capable is this program, structurally, compared to where it started, and compared to where it still needs to go.

There's no single official maturity model this course claims as authoritative — vendors publish their own branded versions. What's useful is the general shape: ad hoc, developing, defined, managed, and optimized, where the program eventually improves itself instead of needing to be reminded.

A program is rarely at the same level everywhere, so score dimensions independently instead of collapsing into one number: stewardship, policy and process, measurement, adoption and culture, and tooling. A program that's managed on measurement but still ad hoc on adoption has a specific, actionable gap a blended score would hide.

An assessment that changes nothing is just an exercise. A weak dimension becomes a Now or Next item on the roadmap from Lesson 21. A dimension that moved up a level becomes evidence in the value realization report from Lesson 22 — proof the budget produced real structural improvement.
Treat the five levels as a shared vocabulary for an honest conversation, not a certification to chase for its own sake. Next: a full case study applying every chapter of this course, start to finish.
